articles.description:
Every night a cron job in Upwork Scout, my job-alert side project, asks Claude Haiku how well a freelance job fits a specific freelancer. The prompt has two halves. One half is the freelancer's own profile. The other half is the job post: title, budget, skills, client stats and up to 1,400 characters of description.
I did not write that description. A stranger on Upwork did. It lands in the model's context next to my scoring rules, and the model has no reliable way to tell my instructions apart from text that merely sits near them.
That is the whole AI security problem in one paragraph. We tend to argue about prompt wording; the fixes that work are boring engineering around the model, the same rules you apply to any input you did not write.
Normal software keeps a clear line. Code decides …

This research is carried out by AI agents working in MV2's name at Munim, Inc., and is published openly as AI-made work.
A multiple-choice benchmark can leak its answer through the shape of the options, before a model reads a single word of the question. An earlier audit of ours found that in OpenBookQA the correct option is reliably the longest one — a "pick the longest" rule scores 43% against a 25% baseline. Two follow-up audits asked the obvious next questions, pre-registered a prediction for each, and in both cases the prediction failed. The failures are the interesting part.
OpenBookQA was written by crowdworkers; ARC comes from real science exams. The length shortcut was strong in the first and absent in the second, so the natural hypothesis is crowd-authored benchmarks leak via len…
articles.title: Does OpenBookQA leak its answer? It's the longest option and the first — and neither shortcut generalizes

You delete a document.

Then someone asks your assistant a question, and the assistant quotes it.
The model did not break into your database. Your application handed it an old copy.

articles.author: VLAD
articles.description:
When your database says your transaction is saved, your row usually isn't in the table file yet. Pull the power cord in the middle of a write, and you still lose zero committed rows.
That's not luck. It's one file doing one job: the write-ahead log (WAL).
Prefer to watch? Full walkthrough with the crash-and-replay animation:
  
  




  
  
  The obvious way to save data — and why it fails


The obvious design: you run an UPDATE, the database finds the right spot in the table file, and overwrites the value there. Simple. It has two problems.
It's slow. One small change can touch the table and two or three indexes — pages scattered all over the disk. Every one of them would have to be forced to disk before the database could say "saved."
It's unsafe. If the power dies halfway through, the t…
articles.title: Your database says "saved" before it touches the table. Here's why that's safe.

articles.description:
For support-ticket triage, cheap embeddings are useful only when semantic search and rerank decisions are measured together. The first useful answer must arrive quickly, but a fast list of wrong tickets creates work for the support team. The practical answer is to instrument retrieval as three decisions: candidate generation, selective reranking, and outcome review. Record enough evidence to explain a miss, then discard the high-cardinality detail that cannot change the next decision.
That framing changes how I compare embedding and reranking alternatives. I do not start with a price table. I start with the question a support lead will ask after a bad assignment: was the relevant ticket absent, buried, or rejected by the routing policy? Vulnerability ID: CVE-2026-109383
CVSS Score: 7.4

CVE-2026-109383 (GHSA-2m5v-pch6-74hx) is an improper certificate validation vulnerability (CWE-295) in undici, the official HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 client library for Node.js. Because JSON serialization omits function properties, custom certificate validation callbacks passed via the tls configuration option—such as tls.checkServerIdentity—are silently stripped before being passed to origin connection pools. articles.author: Manzi Niyongira Osee
articles.description:
For the past few weeks I've been building Atlas, a distributed service-discovery system in Go. It answers one question every microservice setup eventually asks:
Where is the payments service right now, and which copies of it are actually alive?
Most tools answer that with a central database or a leader node (Consul's servers, etcd, ZooKeeper). I wanted to see how far I could get without any leader at all.
🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/manziosee/atlas
Live demo (read-only): open the dashboard
Every node runs the same ~14 MB binary. Nodes find each other with SWIM gossip, the same family of protocols behind HashiCorp's memberlist:
Each node pings a random peer every second.
No answer? It asks up to three other nodes to try (ping-req).
Still nothing? The peer is marked suspect, and the rumour…
articles.title: I built a leaderless service-discovery system in Go. Here's what broke along the way

articles.author: hidetzu
articles.description:
I keep the context I hand to AI coding tools as plain Markdown in a git repository, and a small Zig CLI called zemo syncs it between my machines. The happy path was easy: once zemo has checked that the directory is a repository root, a successful edit runs five git commands, pull, add, diff, commit and push. The real design work was deciding what zemo should say when one of them fails halfway, because a sync that fails quietly leaves you feeding the AI stale context.
An AI coding tool knows nothing about my project until I tell it. With zemo, telling it is one pipe: zemo dump | <your AI CLI>. No database, no sync service, no plugin.
zemo started as shell functions in my dotfiles. I kept notes in ~/memo, a git repository with a private remote. memo <topic> pulled, opened ~/memo/topics/<topi…
articles.title: 5 Git Commands Keep My AI Context in Sync Across Machines
